questions.stem: A patient's blood test shows a low red blood cell count. Which symptom would they most likely experience, and why?

options.text: Frequent infections, because red blood cells fight pathogens
Fatigue and breathlessness, because fewer red blood cells means less oxygen is transported to tissues
Excessive bleeding from cuts
Swollen joints

questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues. Fewer red blood cells means less oxygen delivery, reducing aerobic respiration in cells. This causes fatigue (less energy) and breathlessness (the body tries to compensate by breathing faster). Fighting infections is the role of white blood cells, not red.

questions.stem: Platelets are cell fragments in the blood. At the site of a wound, they clump together and release chemicals that start the clotting process. Why is blood clotting important?

options.text: Clotting provides nutrients to the wound for healing
Clotting forms a scab that seals the wound, preventing blood loss and entry of pathogens
Clotting destroys bacteria directly
Clotting increases blood pressure at the wound site

questions.explanation: Platelets trigger the conversion of fibrinogen (soluble protein in plasma) to fibrin (insoluble threads), which forms a mesh over the wound. This mesh traps red blood cells, forming a clot (scab). The clot stops further blood loss and creates a physical barrier preventing pathogenic microorganisms from entering the body.

questions.stem: White blood cells can be divided into phagocytes and lymphocytes. A phagocyte encounters a bacterium. What does it do?

options.text: It produces antibodies that neutralise the bacterium
It engulfs (phagocytoses) and digests the bacterium using enzymes
It releases antitoxins to neutralise bacterial toxins
It surrounds the bacterium with a membrane to contain it

questions.explanation: Phagocytes are white blood cells that destroy pathogens by phagocytosis -- they engulf the pathogen into a vacuole and digest it using enzymes (lysozymes). This is a non-specific immune response (works against any pathogen). Lymphocytes produce antibodies and antitoxins as part of the specific immune response.

questions.stem: Plasma is the liquid component of blood. Which of the following is NOT transported by plasma?

options.text: Carbon dioxide (as dissolved bicarbonate ions)
Urea (from the liver to the kidneys)
Oxygen (the majority of oxygen transport)
Glucose (from the intestine/liver to body cells)

questions.explanation: While a tiny amount of oxygen dissolves in plasma, the vast majority (about 98%) of oxygen is transported by haemoglobin inside red blood cells, not in the plasma. Plasma does transport dissolved CO2 (as bicarbonate ions), urea, glucose, amino acids, hormones, antibodies, and heat.

questions.stem: A person with haemophilia produces very few functional clotting factors. What is the main risk for this person?

options.text: They will develop more infections
Even minor injuries can lead to prolonged bleeding that is difficult to stop
Their blood will become too thick
They will produce too many red blood cells

questions.explanation: Haemophilia is a genetic condition where the blood lacks certain clotting factors, meaning the clotting cascade cannot complete properly. Even small cuts or internal bruising can cause prolonged bleeding because a stable clot cannot form. Treatment involves regular injections of the missing clotting factor.
